generated_by: hand-curated by the thermal_sim agent from research-notes/storage_devices_supply.md and report/Prescribed drug heat risks.md (14 Nov 2026)
honesty_rule: Advice is defined only as 'within label' / 'beyond label but within what studies tested' / 'beyond what studies tested'. The engine never outputs a '% potency left'. Study percentages below describe what a study measured, not an estimate for any patient's medicine.

advice_tiers.use_as_normal: Within label: every temperature stayed inside the product's labeled storage range (including any excursion the label or USP explicitly allows).
advice_tiers.check_with_pharmacist: Beyond label, but within what studies tested: the exposure went outside the label, and a published study held this product at least this hot for at least this long (at a constant temperature) without a meaningful loss.
advice_tiers.request_replacement: Beyond what studies tested: the exposure went outside the label and no study in our evidence base covers it, or it reached a level where a study found loss or malfunction.

rule_details: Label check: min temperature >= label.min_c AND (peak <= label.max_c OR (label.spike exists AND peak <= spike.max_c AND hours above label.max_c <= spike.max_hours)).

Harm check (checked first): for each evidence item with used_in_rule=true and outcome in {loss, device_failure, measurement_error}: peak >= exposure.temp_c AND hours at or above exposure.temp_c >= exposure.hours -> request_replacement.

Benign envelope: for each evidence item with used_in_rule=true, outcome=no_meaningful_change and exposure.mode=constant: peak <= exposure.temp_c AND hours above label.max_c <= exposure.hours -> check_with_pharmacist.
Below the label minimum (e.g., possible freezing) there is no tested cold envelope in our notes -> request_replacement.
Cyclic studies, studies without a reported temperature, and studies whose IDs are unverified are shown as context but are not used in the rule (used_in_rule=false with a reason).

citation_status_key.verified: PMID/DOI confirmed from PubMed records in research-notes/storage_devices_supply.md
citation_status_key.verified-abstract-only: ID confirmed; only the abstract was read
citation_status_key.listing-only: PMID seen in a PubMed listing; results not read in full
citation_status_key.label-general-knowledge: Typical US prescribing-information / USP wording, written from general knowledge. NOT in the repo research notes. Verify against the dispensed product's label before using clinically.

profiles.name: Insulin pen or vial (e.g., insulin glargine)
profiles.heat_sensitivity: tolerant up to 37 C in trials; untested above 37 C
profiles.mkt_delta_h_note: USP <1079.2> default; no product-specific activation energy in the repo notes.

label.summary: Unopened: refrigerate 2-8 C, do not freeze. Most insulin labels allow keeping a pen/vial unrefrigerated below 30 C (86 F) for a limited number of days (often 28).

evidence.finding: Randomized crossover trial: glargine pens stored at 37 C for 21 days gave the same CGM glucose as refrigerated pens (158.7 vs 157.0 mg/dL, n=40); UHPLC content equal.

citation.text: Kongmalai T et al., BMJ Open Diabetes Res Care 2022

evidence.finding: In-use pens of 4 basal insulins kept 28 days at 29.7 C, 37 C or cycling held 97-101.5% of control content.

citation.text: Kongmalai T et al., Exp Clin Endocrinol Diabetes 2021

evidence.finding: Insulins cycled 25-37 C (refugee-camp profile) for 4 weeks met pharmacopeial standards; bioactivity matched 2-8 C controls.
evidence.why_not_used: cyclic profile; covered by the constant 37 C studies anyway

citation.text: Kaufmann B et al., PLoS One 2021

evidence.finding: Regular, NPH and 70/30 insulin shipped 24-120 h in simulated summer/winter profiles, in non-insulated or gel-pack mailers, all met USP potency.
evidence.why_not_used: profile temperatures not recorded in our notes

citation.text: Chandler C et al., Am J Health Syst Pharm 2008

evidence.finding: Older animal study: rabbits given insulin stored at 32 or 37 C for 28 days showed no significant glucose fall vs 5 C storage; authors concluded potency was lost. Conflicts with the RCT.
evidence.why_not_used: conflicts with the 2022 RCT; abstract not read in full; shown to the pharmacist as a caveat

citation.text: Vimalavathini R, Gitanjali B, Indian J Med Res 2009

profiles.evidence_gaps: No clinical-outcome studies above 37 C (cars, direct sun). Freezing is outside label.
caveats: One older rabbit study (PMID 19797814) reported loss at 32-37 C; the 2022 RCT did not.

advice_text.use_as_normal: Your insulin stayed within its labeled temperature range. Use as normal.
advice_text.check_with_pharmacist: Your insulin got warmer than its label allows, but studies kept insulin pens at 37 C (99 F) for 3-4 weeks without losing effect. Check with your pharmacist before using it, and watch your glucose closely.
advice_text.request_replacement: Your insulin got hotter (or colder) than any study we know of has tested. Request a replacement and ask your pharmacist what to use in the meantime.

profiles.name: Insulin in a pump reservoir / infusion set
profiles.applies_to_note: Filled reservoirs are not shipped; this profile is for insulin already in a pump or a filled reservoir left somewhere hot (home scenarios). Body heat from wearing the pump is not modeled.

label.summary: Pump-use insulin labels typically say to replace insulin in the reservoir every few days and to discard it if exposed to temperatures above 37 C (98.6 F).

evidence.finding: Lispro in a MiniMed pump was chemically stable for 14 days at 37 C.

citation.text: Sharrow SD et al., Diabetes Technol Ther 2012

evidence.finding: Aspart at 37 +/- 2 C for up to 7 days.

citation.text: Senstius J, Diabetes Technol Ther 2007

evidence.finding: In normal wear, reservoir temperature ranged 25-37 C (mean ~30 C), above ambient because of body heat.
evidence.why_not_used: exposure measurement, not a stability outcome

citation.text: Herr JK et al., J Diabetes Sci Technol 2014

evidence.finding: Pump temperature rose 6.4 C during long Li-ion charging and 4.4 C in a 35 C chamber, exceeding 37 C (industry-sponsored; relevance disputed).

citation.text: Vereshchetin P et al., Med Devices (Auckl) 2016

evidence.finding: Case report: diabetic ketoacidosis after an insulin pump was exposed to heat and sunlight.
evidence.why_not_used: German case report; exposure details unknown

citation.text: Pryce R, Praxis (Bern) 2009

profiles.evidence_gaps: No studies of pump insulin above 37 C.

advice_text.use_as_normal: The insulin in your pump stayed at or below 37 C (98.6 F). Use as normal.
advice_text.check_with_pharmacist: The insulin went beyond its label but stayed within what studies tested. Check with your pharmacist or diabetes team.
advice_text.request_replacement: The insulin in your pump/reservoir got hotter than 37 C (98.6 F), beyond what studies tested. Replace the insulin, reservoir and infusion set, and check your glucose more often today.

profiles.name: Epinephrine auto-injector (e.g., 0.3 mg)
profiles.heat_sensitivity: label 20-25 C; lab studies show loss only after days at 70 C

label.summary: Store at 20-25 C; excursions permitted to 15-30 C. Do not refrigerate.

evidence.finding: 25 in-date auto-injectors held at a constant 70 C for 5 days delivered 96.8% of labeled dose.

citation.text: Rachid O et al., Drug Dev Ind Pharm 2016

evidence.finding: Same study: constant 70 C for 10 days delivered 77.7 +/- 3.3% of labeled dose (controls 103.7%).

citation.text: Rachid O et al., Drug Dev Ind Pharm 2016

evidence.finding: Same study: 5 days of cyclic 70 C heating gave 87.2% of labeled dose.
evidence.why_not_used: time at 70 C per cycle not in our notes; a single doorstep event is far shorter than 5 days of cycling

citation.text: Rachid O et al., Drug Dev Ind Pharm 2016

evidence.finding: Systematic review (9 studies): heat degraded epinephrine only with prolonged exposure; real-world fluctuations caused no significant degradation; all 40 auto-injectors tested fired.
evidence.why_not_used: no single exposure level to encode

citation.text: Parish HG et al., Ann Allergy Asthma Immunol 2016

evidence.finding: Pilot: a few hours in a parked car on a sunny summer day lowered epinephrine concentration with no visible change; devices stayed functional (secondary reporting).
evidence.why_not_used: temperature not reported in our notes; ID unverified. Shown to the pharmacist as a caveat.

citation.text: Polish pilot via SnackSafely (2018)

evidence.finding: Auto-injectors heated to about 80-89 C for 8 h and cooled became hard to remove from their carrier tubes in 84% of cases (secondary reporting).
evidence.why_not_used: ID unverified; anything above 70 C is already beyond the tested envelope

citation.text: Seattle-led study via Allergic Living (2020)

evidence.finding: Epinephrine 1:10,000 (0.1 mg/mL) heated to 70 C 8 h/day degraded significantly by 8 weeks (64% by 12 weeks); 1:1,000 (1 mg/mL) was not significantly degraded at 12 weeks. Applies to ampoules/syringes, not auto-injectors; shows dilute concentrations are the fragile ones.
evidence.why_not_used: different product (dilute EMS epinephrine) and cyclic

citation.text: Grant TA et al., Am J Emerg Med 1994

profiles.evidence_gaps: Only 2 small studies involve auto-injectors. No study at realistic doorstep/car profiles with reported temperatures and verified IDs.
caveats: A small pilot (ID unverified) reported lower epinephrine concentration after a few hours in a hot parked car.

advice_text.use_as_normal: Your epinephrine stayed within its labeled temperature range. Keep it with you as normal.
advice_text.check_with_pharmacist: Your epinephrine got warmer than its label allows. Lab studies found auto-injectors still delivered their dose after days at much higher heat, but ask your pharmacist whether to replace it. Keep carrying it until you have a replacement.
advice_text.request_replacement: Your epinephrine was exposed to heat beyond what studies tested. Request a replacement now, and keep this one until the new one arrives: an auto-injector exposed to heat is better than none in an emergency.

profiles.name: Albuterol (salbutamol) HFA inhaler
profiles.heat_sensitivity: storage heat probably tolerated; pressurized canister has a hard limit

label.summary: Store at 15-25 C. Contents under pressure: do not expose to temperatures above 49 C (120 F); the canister may burst.

evidence.finding: Proventil HFA and Ventolin HFA stored 6 months in a car trunk in Tucson: dose delivery not significantly altered once tested at normal temperature; delivery changed when tested (used) outside the recommended range.
evidence.why_not_used: trunk temperatures not recorded in our notes; ID unverified. A measured temperature from this study would likely move doorstep exposures to 'check with your pharmacist'.

citation.text: Hoye WL et al. (University of Arizona)

evidence.finding: Patients carried salbutamol inhalers with loggers 2-3 weeks; authors projected smaller lung doses in hot summer.

citation.text: Aerosol Sci Technol 2016

profiles.evidence_gaps: No study in our notes reports the storage temperature reached together with the outcome.
caveats: Let a hot inhaler return to room temperature before use: delivery changes when the canister itself is hot or cold.

advice_text.use_as_normal: Your inhaler stayed within its labeled temperature range. Use as normal.
advice_text.check_with_pharmacist: Your inhaler got warmer than its label allows but within what studies tested. Let it cool to room temperature and check with your pharmacist.
advice_text.request_replacement: Your inhaler got warmer than its label allows, and no study we hold reports a tested temperature for this. Let it cool to room temperature (do not use it hot), keep it for emergencies, and request a replacement.

profiles.name: Blood glucose test strips
profiles.heat_sensitivity: fragile: reading errors after short heat/humidity exposure
profiles.mkt_delta_h_note: USP <1079.2> default (strips are enzyme reagents, not a drug; MKT shown for comparison only).

label.summary: Brand-specific; commonly about 4-30 C, keep vial capped (humidity). Check the strip vial.

evidence.finding: About 15 minutes at roughly 42 C and 83% RH produced meter bias up to 20 mg/dL and combined error of about 30%.

citation.text: Louie RF et al., J Diabetes Sci Technol 2014

evidence.finding: Strips heat-stressed at 40 C for up to 4 weeks gave elevated results.
Under a 24-h temperature/humidity cycle modeled on post-Katrina conditions, meter errors reached about 22-24%.
evidence.why_not_used: cycle temperatures not in our notes; ID unverified

citation.text: Louie et al., Disaster Med Public Health Prep

profiles.evidence_gaps: No study shows strips are fine after heat beyond their label; direction of error depends on strip chemistry (humidity can push readings the other way).
caveats: Humidity also matters and is not modeled here.

advice_text.use_as_normal: Your test strips stayed within their labeled range. Use as normal.
advice_text.check_with_pharmacist: Your strips went beyond their label but within what studies tested. Run a control-solution test before relying on them.
advice_text.request_replacement: Your test strips got hotter than their label allows; studies found reading errors after short heat exposure. Request replacement strips; until then, confirm unexpected readings with a control-solution test.

profiles.name: GLP-1 receptor agonist pen (e.g., semaglutide, liraglutide, tirzepatide)

label.summary: Refrigerate 2-8 C before first use; do not freeze. Labels differ: some allow limited unrefrigerated storage up to 30 C (86 F) before or after first use; at least one product's unopened label is 2-8 C only. Class-level approximation used here: up to 30 C.

profiles.evidence_gaps: The research notes found no peer-reviewed heat-stability data for GLP-1 pens. Any exposure beyond label is therefore beyond what studies tested.
caveats: Class-level label approximation; verify the specific product's label.

advice_text.use_as_normal: Your pen stayed within its labeled temperature range. Use as normal.
advice_text.check_with_pharmacist: Your pen went beyond its label but within what studies tested. Check with your pharmacist.
advice_text.request_replacement: Your pen got warmer (or colder) than its label allows, and we found no studies testing GLP-1 pens in heat. Request a replacement and ask your pharmacist about this dose.

profiles.name: Room-temperature oral tablets (e.g., metformin, lisinopril) - contrast case
profiles.heat_sensitivity: robust by label: USP allows short spikes to 40 C

label.summary: USP controlled room temperature: 20-25 C, excursions 15-30 C, mean kinetic temperature not above 25 C; transient spikes up to 40 C permitted if they do not exceed 24 hours (USP <659>).

profiles.evidence_gaps: The notes hold no heat-stability studies for common oral tablets. (The only documented toxic heat degradation is historical tetracycline, which involved moisture and age.)

advice_text.use_as_normal: Your tablets stayed within the temperature range their label allows. Use as normal.
advice_text.check_with_pharmacist: Your tablets went beyond their label but within what studies tested. Check with your pharmacist.
advice_text.request_replacement: Your tablets got hotter than 40 C (104 F) or stayed hot longer than the label allows, and we have no study covering that. Ask your pharmacist; most tablets are robust, but this is beyond what we can vouch for.
